newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW - Paris judge on Eurotunnel.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Paris judge on Eurotunnel.

text.p: The president of the Paris commercial court told Reuters on Wednesday he took the initiative to persuade a reluctant Eurotunnel and its negotiating banks to accept the mediation process which led to the breakthrough in debt negotiations.

Jean-Pierre Mattei, Mattei said in a telephone interview he was motivated by considerations of "fairness" to the shareholders and the sheer scale of the financial and legal complications if Eurotunnel SA /Plc failed.

"The scale of Eurotunnel is such that a failure, with its 70 billion francs (debt), an international treaty, two courts involved -- London and Paris -- would have meant a legal and financial imbroglio without precedent," he said.

Mattei asked, as an "exceptional measure," for Eurotunnel's shares to be suspended in London, Paris and Brussels in his capacity as the court president, while the endgame for the talks was being played out.

"We had a duty to succeed and we should be delighted that the negotiators for the banks and Eurotunnel have been able, finally, to reach an agreement under the auspices of Lord Wakeham and Robert Badinter," he said.
But he first had to convince a "hesitant" Eurotunnel and its six banks negotiating for the 225-strong syndicate to accept the court-driven but "friendly" procedure of "mandat ad hoc."

"It was my initiaitve because I explained to the company that if it did not enter into the mandat ad hoc (mediation procedure), unfortunately, the court would have to ask questions about an insolvency," he said.
The company and bankers were unfamiliar with the process but Mattei proposed it as it seemed a "reasonable and pragmatic" solution -- a view he says both sides came to accept in the end.
Mattei said he insisted that Eurotunnel and its bankers stick to his strict sense of timing.
"If things dragged on, failure would have been probable. That's the reason why I reminded everyone with firmness that the timetable had to be kept and everyone had to face up to responsibilities."

He said Eurotunnel's 750,000 shareholders, were, unfortunately, not owed anything under French as well as English law. "But if they were abandoned by the banks, I think it is an attack on equity. And I mean equity, I am not talking of justice," he said.
Equity is a concept in English jurisprudence concerning the essential fairness of a case.
Shareholders, holders of risk capital, face losing everything as their dividends are not guaranteed and they stand behind banks, who hold security on assets, in an insolvency.
"I do not believe one can or should abandon on the roadside 750,000 shareholders who placed their confidence in the banks and in a European project as extraordinary as Eurotunnel.
